food.text: Elena Molokhovets's A Gift to Young Housewives, first published in 1861, was the best-selling Russian cookbook of the 19th century. It contains nine recipes for borscht, some of them based on kvass, a traditional Slavic fermented beverage made from rye bread.

The humble potato became so common in Belarus in the 19th century that more than 300 potato dishes have been recorded there. It came to be considered the core ingredient of the national cuisine, and draniki, pancakes of grated potato, are often seen as a signature dish.

Potatoes first appeared in Dnieper Ukraine in the mid-18th century and were gradually adopted in the countryside. By the mid-19th century they were grown in all povits of Kyiv, Chernihiv and Poltava Governorates, and a rich peasant from the Chyhyryn area would eat 150 kg of them per year.

Nineteenth-century Russian and Polish cookbooks, such as Yekaterina Avdeyeva's Handbook of the Experienced Russian Housewife (1842) and Wincenta Zawadzka's The Lithuanian Cook (1854), called beetroot borscht "Little Russian borscht". That name suggests the innovation took place in what is now Ukraine, whose soils and climate suit beet cultivation.
In 1845, more than 600 tons of potatoes were harvested on suburban land plots in Kyiv. That was still not enough, so the city had to import one cart of potatoes per inhabitant every year on average.

In 1878, Maria Marciszewska published the cookbook Kucharka szlachecka in Zhytomyr, calling herself a "Lithuanian living in Ukraine". Her recipe bore the double name "Lithuanian cold soup, or Ukrainian cold soup", showing how far the dish had spread across regions.

Pelmeni began to appear in restaurants in late 19th-century France, when Russian dishes had already made a considerable impact on haute cuisine. Auguste Escoffier included them in Le Guide Culinaire as a hot hors d'oeuvre, which was contrary to the Russian custom.

Ukrainian legends, probably of 19th century origin, credit the invention of beetroot borscht to Cossacks. One version names Zaporozhian Cossacks serving in the Polish army on their way to break the siege of Vienna in 1683, another names Don Cossacks laying siege to Azov in 1695.

In the 19th century, Jewish influence on Belarusian cooking was especially noticeable in bringing in potato dishes of German origin, such as babka. The exchange went both ways, since the famous bulbe latkes, the potato pancakes of the East European Jews, may have been borrowed from the Belarusian draniki.

Ukrainians started adding potatoes to soups and ukha in the first half of the 19th century. The addition of potatoes to borshch was first mentioned in 1853 in the area of Khorol near Poltava, and by the early 20th century varenyky filled with potatoes were a usual dish around Lubny.

Adam Kirkor's "Ethnographic View on the Vilna Governorate" (1857) described summer foods including bread kvass and kholodnik. This cold soup was prepared with steamed greens, light kvass, salt, and milk.

Marciszewska also recorded a Lenten cold beet soup. Because sour cream and meat were forbidden during fasting periods, she used crayfish tails and olive oil instead, and whitened the soup with milk made from dried walnuts.

art.text: Russian architecture kept changing style through the 1800s. Under Alexander I the Empire style became the de facto architectural style, and Nicholas I opened the gate of Eclecticism to Russia. The second half of the century was dominated by the Neo-Byzantine and Russian Revival style.

The first known opera made in Russia was A Life for the Tsar by Mikhail Glinka, in 1836. Ruslan and Lyudmila followed in 1842. Russian opera was originally a combination of Russian folk music and Italian opera.

Russian lacquer art grew out of icon painting. Icon painters who had supplied churches and homes needed a new living, so they made papier-mâché boxes and panels, lacquered them and painted them by hand. During the nineteenth century the artists began painting idealized scenes of the country and peasant life, as well as folk tales.

The Russian painters known as the Peredvizhniki, or wanderers, broke with the Russian Academy and started a school of art free from Academic restrictions. Realism dominated 19th-century Russian art. Under Alexander II critical realism flourished, with artists showing the conditions of the poor and caricaturing authority, and some making the circle of human suffering their main theme. Leading realists included Ivan Shishkin, Ilya Repin and Isaac Levitan.

Nineteenth-century Russian music was defined by a tension between two camps. On one side stood Mikhail Glinka and The Mighty Handful, and on the other the Russian Musical Society led by composers Anton and Nikolay Rubinstein. Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's later tradition was carried into the 20th century by Sergei Rachmaninoff.

The village of Fedoskino, near Moscow on the banks of the Ucha River, is the oldest of the four centers of Russian lacquer miniature painting, practiced there since 1795. It stands apart because its artists use oil paints rather than egg tempera. Its style is largely realistic in composition and detail.

Ukrainian sculptors of the 19th century often studied at imperial academies in Saint Petersburg, Vienna, Kraków or Prague. They worked within academic and salon sculpture, producing portrait busts, allegorical compositions and public monuments. Projects to commemorate Taras Shevchenko and Cossack leaders were begun, though many faced political obstacles under imperial rule.

Art Nouveau in Ukrainian lands was influenced by two major schools: the Vienna Secession and French Moderne. Major examples include the railway stations in Zhmerynka and Lviv, and civic and residential buildings in Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa.

A lubok is a Russian popular print with simple graphics and narratives drawn from literature, religious stories and popular tales, used as decoration in houses and inns. From the mid-19th century, lithography was used to make them. They sometimes appeared in series, which might be seen as predecessors of the modern comic strip.

From 1900, a new national architectural style emerged in Ukraine, inspired by folk architecture and Ukrainian Baroque. Its works include the Intercession Church in Plishyvets near Poltava (1902) and the Poltava Governorate Zemstvo Building (1901–1908). Vasyl Krychevsky was its most prominent architect.

The neoclassical building of Kyiv's National Art Museum was constructed in 1898 by architect Władysław Horodecki. Its facade has a six-column Doric porch with a frieze depicting the Triumph of Arts. Gryphons and large concrete lions at the top of the stairs were created by the Italian sculptor Emilio Sala.

The Lviv National Art Gallery holds the largest collection of Jan Matejko's work outside Poland. It includes major historical themes and intimate family paintings such as Portrait of the Artist's Children, from 1879. The gallery's founding decision came in 1897, and it first formally opened in 1907.
art.source_title: Borys Voznytsky Lviv National Art Gallery

art.text: The building of the Kyiv museum cost 249,000 rubles, but the imperial government paid only 100,000. The Tereshchenko family paid another 108,000 rubles. The museum officially opened in December 1904 as the Kyiv Industrial Arts and Science museum of Emperor Nicholas II, and its first director was Mykola Biliashivsky.

The Potocki Palace in Lviv was completed in 1890 and designed by the French architect Louis Dovern. Władysław Łoziński's Palace was built in 1872–1874 by architect F. Pokutynsky, and was the site of the original 1907 gallery institution.
art.source_title: Borys Voznytsky Lviv National Art Gallery

war.text: Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 is recognized as one of the most devastating military endeavors ever. In less than six months the campaign claimed the lives of around a million soldiers and civilians. Of Napoleon's army, about 380,000 were dead or missing/prisoner, roughly half from disease, and more than half of the soldiers in the retreat perished from starvation, exhaustion, typhus and the unforgiving climate. In Russia it is known as the Patriotic War of 1812.

The Caucasian War was a 19th-century conflict between the Russian Empire and peoples of the North Caucasus who resisted subjugation. The Russian Imperial Army and Cossack settlers waged a series of military actions against native inhabitants such as the Adyghe, Abazins, Ubykhs, Chechens and Dagestanis as the Tsars sought to expand. It spanned the reigns of three successive tsars: Alexander I, Nicholas I and Alexander II. Warfare finally ended between 1856 and 1859, and its resumed phase after 1833 marked the beginning of what is now referred to as the Circassian genocide.

The Russo-Japanese War began on 9 February 1904 with a Japanese surprise attack on the Russian Pacific Fleet at Port Arthur. The war ended with the Treaty of Portsmouth in September 1905, mediated by US president Theodore Roosevelt.

In 1914 the Battle of Galicia pitted Russia against Austria-Hungary early in World War I. Austro-Hungarian losses were enormous: Holger Herwig estimates 100,000 dead, 220,000 wounded and 100,000 captured, while Prit Buttar counts 324,000 men lost, including 130,000 prisoners, against 225,000 Russian losses. The Austro-Hungarian armies were forced out of Galicia and the battle killed a large portion of their trained officers, while the Russians captured Lemberg, now Lviv, and then ruled Eastern Galicia for approximately nine months.

Napoleon crossed the Neman River on 24 June 1812 with an army of nearly half a million men. He faced Russian forces led by Barclay de Tolly and Pyotr Bagration, totaling roughly 180,000 to 220,000 soldiers. He captured Smolensk after a two-day battle in August, but the main Russian armies escaped encirclement. Even before this, the army had suffered enormous losses from extreme weather, disease, desertion and inadequate supplies. In the first eight weeks, before any major battle, the Grande Armée shrank by a third, from diseases such as diphtheria, dysentery and typhus and from starvation, and more than 5,000 dead horses were left in its wake on the way to Vilnius.

The Russian Baltic Fleet sailed over seven months and 18,000 nautical miles from the Baltic Sea to reinforce the Pacific Fleet, reaching the Sea of Japan in May 1905. The Japanese Combined Fleet intercepted it at the Battle of Tsushima on 27-28 May 1905 and virtually annihilated it. The Russians lost eight battleships, numerous smaller vessels and more than 5,000 men, while the Japanese lost three torpedo boats and 116 men. Only three Russian vessels escaped to Vladivostok.

The war against Napoleonic France compelled Alexander I to reform the Russian military, and in 1802 he created the Ministries of War and the Navy. Even so, Napoleon pummeled a joint Austro-Russian force at Austerlitz in 1805. Russia began to rebound in the War of the Fourth Coalition, fighting an inconclusive battle at Eylau in February 1807.

In the final phase of the Caucasian War, a 250,000 strong army under General Baryatinsky broke the mountaineers' resistance. The Russians had brokered a truce with Shamil during the Crimean War, but hostilities resumed in 1855. In the east the Russians captured Shamil in 1859, forced him to surrender and swear allegiance to the Tsar, and exiled him to Central Russia. The war in the west continued against the Circassians until a manifesto of Tsar Alexander II declared hostilities at an end on June 2 (May 21 OS), 1864.

The Caucasian War drew in famous writers. Leo Tolstoy gained much of his knowledge of war for War and Peace from these encounters. Mikhail Lermontov fought in the battle near the river Valerik, which inspired a poem of the same name.

Russian historians have long focused on 1812 rather than the later campaigns. Lieven observed that for every book on the campaigns of 1813 to 1814 there are a hundred on 1812. Tolstoy ended War and Peace in December 1812, ignoring the campaigns that ended with the Russians marching into Paris.

Russian service in the army was for life for most of the 18th century. It was changed to 25 years in 1793 and gradually shortened after the Napoleonic Wars. By 1855 it stood at twelve years of active service plus three years in the reserve.

literature.text: Ukrainian literature developed mostly under foreign domination, ruled by powers such as the Russian Empire and the Austro-Hungarian Empire. From the 19th century, Ukrainian literary works started to be written in a colloquial form, and poems, novels and plays were published. Nationalist and independence movements grew alongside this trend. The Russian Empire and the Soviet Union that followed it often suppressed and restricted the use of the Ukrainian language, its methods of expression and its literary subjects.

From the early 1830s, Russian literature underwent an astounding Golden Age in poetry, prose and drama. The Romantic movement contributed to a flowering of talent, as the poet Vasily Zhukovsky and later his protégé Alexander Pushkin came to the fore.
Russian symbolism was the first Silver Age development, emerging in the 1890s. It arose largely separately from West European symbolism, emphasizing the mysticism of Sophiology and defamiliarization.

Russia issued two notorious decrees against Ukrainian-language publishing. The Valuev Circular of 1863 banned religious and educational books in Ukrainian. The Ems Ukaz of 1876, issued by Tsar Alexander II, extended the ban to virtually all original works and translations, including theatrical performances and song lyrics.

Under the restrictions, Ukrainian-language printing in the Russian Empire was driven underground or moved to Galicia under Austro-Hungarian rule. The Shevchenko Scientific Society, founded in 1873, and the Prosvita society became the principal Ukrainian publishers in Lviv. The first Kyiv edition of Taras Shevchenko's Kobzar could only appear in 1889 because of these restrictions.

The Ukrainian school was a group of early 19th-century Polish Romantic poets from the southeastern fringes of the Polish-inhabited lands. Antoni Malczewski, Józef Bohdan Zaleski, Tomasz Padura, Aleksander Groza and Seweryn Goszczyński worked Ukrainian life, landscapes, history and folklore into their poetry, creating a distinct style of Polish Romanticism.

In Galicia, the Eastern Catholic clergy were heavily involved in spreading literacy. Of 43 Ukrainian-language books published in Galicia between 1837 and 1850, 40 were written by members of the clergy. The Ukrainian author Ivan Belei remarked that Galician Rus may be the only place in the world where neither literature nor politics is possible without priestly support.

The Russian Revolution of 1905 partly relaxed imperial censorship, and Ukrainian-language newspapers, journals and books appeared legally in Dnieper Ukraine for the first time in decades. The literary monthly Literaturno-Naukovyi Vistnyk moved its editorial offices from Lviv to Kyiv in 1907 under Mykhailo Hrushevsky. Renewed restrictions from 1910 to 1914 narrowed the field again.

Ukrainian school poets in turn influenced both Lithuanian and Ukrainian Romantic poetry. Along with other Polish poets, they formed a link between the various literatures of the post-partition Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

Priests actively supported the first Ukrainian newspaper, Zorya Halytska, meaning Galician Star, by reading it aloud to illiterate peasants or having their cantors do so. The first West Ukrainian grammar was published by a priest who also translated Goethe and Schiller into Ukrainian.

In 1892 Ivan Franko presented a work on Ukrainian literature of the 16th to 18th centuries, opposing Russian imperial claims that literature in Ukrainian lands could only lie in union with Russia. He argued its chronology should begin not from 1798 but from the Medieval era. Russian scholars such as Alexander Pypin denied Ukrainian literature's descent from Rus' literary works.

Between 1909 and 1912, Bohdan Lepky, a professor at the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, published two volumes on the history of Ukrainian literature up to the time of Ivan Kotliarevsky. A third volume was destroyed in 1914 during the Russian invasion of Galicia.

Extensive castigation of nihilism found its place in Russian publications and a burgeoning trend of antinihilistic literature. Early examples include Aleksey Pisemsky's Troubled Seas (1863), Nikolai Leskov's No Way Out (1864), and Viktor Klyushnikov's The Mirage (1864).

science.text: Alexander Mozhaysky made his first attempt to fly in a monoplane of his own design as early as 1881. He is remembered as a pioneer of aviation, and his attempt marks the start of the history of Russian aircraft engineering.

Russian science fiction emerged in the mid-19th century, and spaceflight became a central topic from the 1890s. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky wrote In the Moon in 1893 and Dreams of Earth and Skies in 1895. Other writers described voyages in space, including Leonid Bogoyavlensky's Voyage to Mars in 1901.

Ukraine's modern technology grew as railways and the discovery of iron ore and coal launched industrial capitalism in the 19th century. Yet machine building was poorly developed in the Russian Empire, and almost all complex machines were imported. Ukraine's strengths lay in road and bridge building.

Konstantin Tsiolkovsky (1857–1935) published the first serious scientific work on space travel in 1903. His work was essentially unknown outside the Russian Empire, but inside the country it inspired research and the formation of the Society for Studies of Interplanetary Spaceflight.

Ilya Mechnikov was a pioneer in investigations of the immune system. His work earned him the 1908 Nobel Prize in Medicine. He was one of several Russian scientists whose biology research shaped the modern field.

In 1892, the first electric tram line of the Russian Empire started running in Kyiv. It was the third in the world. Kyiv's later Funicular, built in 1902 to 1905, linked the Uppertown with the lower commercial neighborhood of Podil.

The chain bridge over the Dnieper was built in 1847 to 1853 to a project by E. Vignel. Later, from 1898 to 1902, a high bow gauge bridge and a tunnel near Yaremcha in the Carpathians were built. Power stations followed in Kiev in 1890 and in Kharkov in 1897.

Several Russian scientists wrote fiction about future progress. Electric engineer Vladimir Chikolev published "Wonders of Electricity" in 1884, and biologist Porfiry Bakhmetyev wrote "Billionaire's Testament" in 1904. Astronomer Daniil Svyatsky co-authored Islands of Ethereal Ocean in 1914.

Engineers trained at polytechnic schools did the best technical work in Ukraine. Lviv Polytechnic was founded in 1845, followed by the Kharkiv Polytechnic Institute from 1883 and the Kiev Polytechnic Institute from 1898.
In 1881, the Russian revolutionary and rocket pioneer Nikolai Kibalchich proposed pulsed rocket propulsion by combustion of explosives. It was an early precursor for Project Orion.

politics.text: At its height in the late 19th century, the Russian Empire covered about 22,800,000 square kilometres, roughly one-sixth of the world's landmass. That made it the third-largest empire in history, behind only the British and Mongol empires. The 1897 census counted 126 million people.

In 1861 Alexander II, who reigned from 1855 to 1881, emancipated all 23 million serfs in the Russian Empire. It was the most notable of the major reforms he initiated, which followed Russia's defeat in the Crimean War.

Imperial Russia forced Jews to live within the Pale of Settlement, which mainly covered Poland, Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova and Lithuania. Jews could leave it only by converting or by obtaining a university diploma or first guild merchant status.

Alexander I, who reigned from 1801 to 1825, helped defeat the militaristic ambitions of Napoleon. When Napoleon invaded in 1812, the Russians used a scorched earth strategy so the invaders could not live off the land, and the Grande Armée was decimated during the harsh Russian winter. Thousands of French troops were ambushed and killed by peasant guerrilla fighters. Alexander also constituted the Holy Alliance, which aimed to restrain the rise of secularism and liberalism across Europe.

A wave of anti-Jewish riots swept southwestern Russia from 1881 to 1882, with more than 200 events, and made the word pogrom common in English. Thousands of Jewish homes were destroyed, many families were reduced to poverty, and large numbers of men, women, and children were injured in 166 towns. The Kiev pogrom of 26 April 1881 was considered the worst. At least 40 Jews were killed between April and December 1881, and the riots indirectly gave a significant boost to the early Zionist movement.

philosophy.text: In the early 20th century, a new Buddhist temple called Datsan Gunzechoinei was built in Saint Petersburg. It became the northernmost Buddhist temple in Russia, showing how far the religion had spread from its Siberian and Mongolian strongholds.

Russian cosmism was a philosophical and cultural movement that emerged in late 19th- and early 20th-century Russia. It blended science, religion, and metaphysics into one worldview built on belief in humanity's cosmic destiny and the potential for immortality.

The Russian nihilist movement was a philosophical, cultural, and revolutionary movement in the Russian Empire. The word nigilizm came to represent its unremitting attacks on morality, religion, and traditional society, and the movement arose from young radicals disillusioned with earlier social reformers.

Nikolai Fyodorovich Fyodorov (1828–1903) is regarded as the father of Russian cosmism. His philosophy of Humankind's Common Task aimed to regulate the forces of nature, defeat death and bring ancestors back to life so that they too would take part in the general resurrection.

Russian nihilism saw the morality, philosophy, religion, aesthetics, and social institutions then in place as worthless. It incorporated hard determinism, atheism, materialism, positivism, and egoism, but did not necessarily see meaninglessness in all ethics, knowledge, and human life.

Peter Kropotkin, as stated in the Encyclopædia Britannica, defined nihilism as the symbol of struggle against all forms of tyranny, hypocrisy, and artificiality and for individual freedom. This paints the movement as a fight for liberty as well as a rejection of tradition.

Tsiolkovsky wrote a book called "The Will of the Universe; Unknown Intelligent Forces", in which he propounded a philosophy of panpsychism. He did not believe in traditional religious cosmology, but believed in a cosmic being that governed humans, and he thought humans would eventually colonize the Milky Way.

The Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls Russian nihilism the intellectual pool of the period 1855–1866, out of which later radical movements emerged. The movement's countercultural aspects scandalized the country, and even minor indiscretions left nihilists imprisoned for lengthy periods or exiled to Siberia.

In 1864, Fyodor Dostoevsky published Notes from Underground as a direct satire upon Chernyshevsky's novel. Its protagonist both criticizes and parodies Chernyshevsky's views on egoism, presenting a dislikable glorifier of self-will as a more realistic egoist.

culture.text: Tea became a central part of Russian life, and the samovar was widely used to boil water for brewing until the middle of the 20th century. In the 19th century, Russians drank their tea with a cube of sugar from a sugarloaf held between their teeth. The tradition still exists today.

In Galicia, Ukrainian Greek Catholic priests formed a tight-knit hereditary caste of roughly 2,000 to 2,500 by the 19th century. They spread literacy and education in the countryside. Between 1842 and 1856, about 1,000 parish schools were established in the Lviv eparchy.

Odesan Russian is a vernacular variety of Russian with significant Ukrainian and Yiddish substrates. According to the 1897 census, Yiddish was the second most widely spoken language in Odesa, spoken by about 30% of the population. The city's Jews were not confined to ghettos and were much more secularised than Jews elsewhere in the Russian Empire.

Tea caravans carried Chinese tea to Russia, with the Kiakhta tea trade peaking in 1824 and the caravans peaking in 1860. After the first leg of the Trans-Siberian Railway was completed in 1880, faster trains cut the journey from 16 months to seven weeks. By 1905, horse-drawn tea transport had ended.
By the late 19th century, Wissotzky Tea had become the most prominent tea firm in the Russian Empire. By the early 20th century, it was the largest tea manufacturer in the world.

By the mid-19th century, tea had won over the town class, the merchants and the petty bourgeoisie. This is reflected in the dramas of Alexander Ostrovsky. Earlier, the literati of the Karamzinian circle had made tea a significant element of cultural life.

Priests actively supported the first Ukrainian newspaper, Zorya Halytska, either reading it aloud to illiterate peasants or having their cantors do so. Of 43 Ukrainian-language books published in Galicia between 1837 and 1850, 40 were written by members of the clergy.

In 1831, seminarians were required by the head of the Church to take classes in agronomy, since they were expected to introduce modern farming methods to the peasants. Many priests used their lands as model farms. In one region, priests planted the first apricot orchards.
An 1895 sampler of Odesan speech appears in the feuilleton "Odesan Language" by journalist Vlas Doroshevich. Yevgeny Golubovsky credits Doroshevich with inventing the term "Odesan language".
